summary: Find all unique combinations of candidates (reusable any number of times) that sum to the target.
mainInsight: Choose candidates in non-decreasing index order (a start index prevents permutations of the same multiset) and allow reuse by recursing with the SAME index; stop when the remaining sum hits 0 or goes negative.

approaches.name: Backtracking with a start index
approaches.summary: choose(start, remaining): for i >= start try candidates[i], recurse with i.

personalSolution.approach: Backtracking with a start index (reuse via same index)
personalSolution.notes: Optimal pattern; sorting + break prunes more.

promptVariants: How do you avoid generating the same combination in different orders?
What does the start index do?
options: Only consider candidates at index >= start (non-decreasing choice order)
Generate every ordering and then sort the final list of results
Store each combination as a tuple in a set and de-duplicate at the end
Use BFS over partial combinations so duplicate orders merge
cards.answer: Only consider candidates at index >= start (non-decreasing choice order)
cards.explanation: A combination is built in a canonical index order, so [2,3] and [3,2] are not both generated.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Generate every ordering and then sort th: Works but wastes time generating duplicates.

promptVariants: Why recurse with `i` (not `i + 1`) in Combination Sum?
How does this differ from Combination Sum II?
cards.answer: Reusing the same candidate is allowed, so after choosing candidates[i] the next choice may again be candidates[i] (start = i). In Combination Sum II each candidate may be used once, so the recursion uses i + 1 (and duplicates must be skipped).
cards.explanation: The start index still prevents reordering.

promptVariants: Time complexity in terms of N candidates, target T and minimum candidate M: ___
Complete the statement: Time complexity in terms of N candidates, target T and minimum candidate M: ___
cards.explanation: The recursion depth is at most T/M with up to N branches per level.

promptVariants: What is the auxiliary space excluding the output?
How much auxiliary memory does Combination Sum need besides the result?
cards.answer: O(T/M): the depth of the recursion and the length of the current combination.
cards.explanation: The output can be exponentially large.

promptVariants: Why check `remaining < 0` first and how could sorting improve pruning?
cards.answer: Overshooting means this branch cannot succeed, so return. If candidates are sorted, once candidates[i] > remaining all later candidates also overshoot, so you can `break` instead of recursing and returning each time. path[:] snapshots the current combination because path keeps being mutated.

promptVariants: What does the function return for candidates = [2], target = 1?
options: [] (an empty list: no combination sums to the target)
[[]] because the empty combination has a sum of zero
None because there is no valid combination to return
An error is raised because the target is smaller than every candidate
cards.answer: [] (an empty list: no combination sums to the target)
cards.explanation: No combination sums to 1, so no path is ever recorded.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[]] because the empty combination has a: That would claim the empty combination sums to 1.
